INSTITUTE OF JAZZ STUDIES

JAZZ ORAL HISTORY PROJECT
National Endowment for the Arts
Interview with Machito (Frank Grillo)
Conducted by Max Salazar
May, 1980
PROCEEDINGS
When were you born?
The truth?
The truth.
Okay, the date and the year?
'The year is 16th February 1930 - uh - 1908.
Okay, and what was your mother and father's name?
Well, Martha and Rogelio.
Okay, how many children did your family have?
Six
What were their names?
Uhh - Anisa; - it was after me ....
You were the first born in the family?
Yes
Okay, go ahead.
... Anisa, Estela, Graciela, ahh Marta y Rogelio.
Okay, as far as you know, what is the nationality makeup on your father's side?
Well, my father and mother were Cuban.
Uh - huh?
Yes
And their ancestry?
Ahh from my mother's side there was a black African and a Spanish person, you know, my grandfather was Spanish.
And on your father's side?
On my father side my grandmother was a mulata and my grandfather was black.
Uh huh. Macho, what do you remember about your early childhood in Havana?
Well, Havana was so musical, so gay - I mean, so full of life, that I, I don't know, I never had a moment that I, that was a sad moment because that was very happy, very happy era.
Okay, do you remember anything, let's say, from the age five? Do you remember when you were five years old?
Oh, when I was five my father was selling glasses, they was coming from Europe.
Eye-glasses or water-glasses?

Eye - no - water-glasses; and you know, was a big case with a lot of stuff, with some kind of thing in order to preserve the glasses and I guess I got a match and I set a fire to all of them, Where we lived, that was completely destroyed by a fire so everybody hit me in the neighborhood.
Macho, did you live in one of the solares or did you live in an apartment?
No, first I lived in a solar, you know, one of those .....
Where mostly Afro-Cubans live?
Afro-Cubans live.
Okay, do you remember the name of the solar and what district?
It was the Jesus Maria. They called it
el solar de los carretones. The, you know, the buggy - buggy solar.
Uh - huh. And what were your favorite games as a child? Do you remember?
Baseball, boxing - as a matter of fact, I saw Jack Johnson and Jess Willard fight.
You saw the Jess Willard - Jack Johnson fight. What do you remember about that? Who took you to the fight?
My father.
Ah - ha - And do you have any memories of what happened that day?

Well, there was so much commotion, it was in the daytime, it was so hot, you know, I was very very little, you know, but I remember when Willard, there was about 15 or 20 rounds, maybe more, it was a long fight, but that was very funny, very funny to me; naturally I didn't have too much knowledge about fighting, but I saw Jack Johnson when he put up his glove to cover, cover up the sun with the glove - you know, it looked funny and everybody was saying that it was a fake.
I see. Did - - Was that the impression with most of the people? That Jack Johnson threw that fight?
Oh - definetely.
I see. Macho, at that time when you were five years old, Were you living in the solar?
Yes
Okay, describe to me your home and
how many children were living there with you and your mother.
Well by that time we were two. The rest - they - we moved across the street.
So you and Anisa were born in the solar. Right? And how many rooms did you have in el solar?
We had two.
Two rooms.
Two rooms; one for my father - one for Alicia and myself.
So how long do you remember living in el solar before you moved across the street?
Well, I was maybe about nine or ten. And then my father start the business that was, that made him made him very rich.
What business was that?
They were selling groceries.
Tell me about that.

Oh, that was very complicated thing for people. In those days like all these countries they have representation of merchandise: automobiles or whatever, electrical appliances. There were - so we didn't manufacture anything in Cuba, we was buying everything from the United States and from Spain; and from Europe a few things; and from China, the silk. All those stores they was owned by chinamen. They brought all those merchandise from China. - So my father have a lot of trucks or whatever and he used to transport from the - from the docks to the - to the business.
To the business site eh?
Yes, all the merchandise. We . . . .
So he was selling silks and what else?
And groceries
And groceries - For instance give me some examples. What kind of groceries?
Well, the groceries was rice, beans, lard, pork, you know, eh - what you call it - bacon, ham, that was coming from the United States - from Armour and Swift.
He had a street - - He was a street vendor?
Yes - - Yeah, he had a lot of vendors in the street.
Oh, he had people working for him too.
Working for him
I see. Okay, now at that time while this is going on, You were aware of music?

Naturally, because my father was a good singer. You know, when I heard Panchito Riset for the first time, I remembered my father; my father had that type of voice, like Panchito Riset, when he was very young; and my house was a musical house because the day of my mother's birthday was a happy thing there, day before, the day and the day after. So we had Maria Teresa, we had Floro and Miguel, we had all the singers, all the popular singers in Havana. They was coming to my house to sing and celebrate my mother's birthday; and then Calabaza, la orquesta Calabaza, Antonio Maria Romeu and you name it, practically everyone.
Your father used to hire these musicians . . . .
Right.
And they used to play inside your house?
Yes
And who else used to go to the party?

Well, practically everyone. All the people that he was doing business with and the people in the neighborhood because my father was a very liberal guy. There was a lot of poor people. He was practically the only one, rich one in the neighborhood because it was a very,very poor neighborhood.
Okay,Macho. Who were you aware of musically at that time? - when you were about nine or ten. Who was saying anything to you?
Well, ah - - Maria Teresa and - - Maria Teresa, Floro, Floro Zorilla, he was a good singer.
Maria Teresa Vera?
Maria Teresa Vera. That was ah ----
They came after el Sexteto Habanero, am I right?
No, before.
They came before. Okay.
Before, I am talking about ten - when I was - ten years. The Habanero came about 1922, so that was twelve years after.
Okay. All right, politically, What do you remember about that time period when you were about ten years old?
Well, at that time I think that Jose Miguel Gomez was the president and then after that was Zayas and then after that was Menocal.
Okay - Jose Miguel Gomez, What do you remember about him at all?

Well, he was a general in the - in the army. He was one of the helped to liberate Cuba from Spain and naturally all those generals they was the first to become president in Cuba because they had record, good record. They was heroes so .....
Uh Huh - Macho, when did you first become aware of discrimination in Cuba? About how old were you?

Well, when I was seventeen. I never had, never feel the pressure because I - we don't have - I don't have to work to live. I went to school with the Prio Socarras brothers, the small ones. We went to a private school. I had no problems. My economy liberate me. Like it always happen in every country; when you had economy you don't feel as much pressure.
In other words, your father's business made you one of the fortunate Afro-Cubans uh? - - -
Absolutely
- - - - who were better off than the average ones. But when were you - tell me about this time that you became aware of the discrimination against Afro-Cubans.

Well, when I start working. Well, I heard about it, but I never, I never went through the - the - I mean physically or spiritually, whatever; so when I start really making living for myself, because I quit school, and I don't want to ask my father anything, I want to make my own living, so I went to work with Maria Teresa, We used to work at the Academia El Encanto and they - there was a restriction.
We just couldn't talk with nobody, especially with the women, they were white; and a certain restriction that make you aware that their world was different that the one that I used to live.
In other words, You had a different door that you had to come in through? And you had to leave that way too?
Yeah.
What about fountains of water? Did they have one for whites and one for blacks?

No, no, no, no it just was that we - they didn't want us to be mixing with the - with the costumer and with the people they consider that we don't supposed to because I, I don't know, it was so silly.
Was this for the white Cuban also? He couldn't mix with the costumer?
No, the white Cuban . . .
_ the white Cuban musicians -
Yes. Those - they had more privileges that what we had, but still, there was kind of restriction for them too because the costumer they were jealous about
you know, the women like the musicians. They like to talk to them, ask for numbers and this and that, and there was in a way, more to prefer the working class not be mixed......
Mixing with the elite or society.
With the elite, that's right.
Okay. Before that Macho, What do you remember about school? What -- What did you do in school?

Well, I was in private school so I think I was the only Afro-Cuban, really dark fellow - oh another fellow that it was dark too - that his father was white and he owned a sugar mill in Santa Clara; so we was the only ones dark-complexioned in that particular school. Ah - Prió Socarras, the two small brothers, because the president was older, but we went together; were taking bachillerato, what they call a B. A.
There wasn't - we was in private school, but got to take the examination at the Instituto Havana.
At this time Macho, Were you singing or did you have any music inclination - - -
Oh yes
On your mind? Okay, tell me - - -

As a matter of fact, I went through a school of music; my mother used to take me and I used to get from one door and get from the other one. My mother thought that I was in the school and I was going to the movie or whatever, you know, running away from the - from the one thing that I really, I miss it now because I found out through the years that education is simplification of life.
Okay Macho, At that time were there any popular musicians who were idols in Cuba when, let's say, when you were ten or twelve?
Well, El Moro, a flute player - - -
El Moro - - -
One of the best - - -
M-o-r-r-o, El Moro.

El Moro - and there was Panchito, "Flauta Magica" - was El Rubio, those those fellows. El Rubio was a flute player from - from - he played with Antonio Maria Romeu; and then when the Rubio organized a jazz band to go to one of the high-class nightclub - ah ah - Antonio Maria Romeu took the "Flauta Magica", Panchito.
What was the popular music in Cuba at that time?
At that time, Charanga.
Were - - They were playing the Danzon?
Danzon, strictly danzon.
Okay, at that time, Did you know or hear of anything about - ah - the son?
El son come from Oriente, you know close to Guantanamo, whatever, Oriente.
Was it popular then? When you were growing up?

We don't know about it; there was a war, a civil war like - created by Maximo Gomez, in Santiago de Cuba, that became black fighting against white. Evaristo Tenor and few veterans from the liberation army and he create that in order - - -
Who created?
Maximo Gomez, I mean, Jose Miguel Gomez.
Was he white Cuban or black Cuban?
He was a - he was a half-breed.
I see. And what was his reason for creating this friction between whites and blacks?
In order to - to to disturb the political campaign to ah - you know, to create panic.
Was he running for office?
Yes, he was running. He wanted to be elected.
So he needed a cause to get reelected.
Absolutely.
So, tell me what happened.

So, when that thing started in Santiago de Cuba, he sent the regular army from Havana to Santiago de Cuba to stop the revolution, and Godines, that was the first tres player, the guitar player with Sexteto Habanero, and few other guys - they was so rhythmical - the economy was very bad in those days - so they went out there and they learned how to play the tres in Santiago de Cuba.
I see. The soldiers from Havana went there and they learned how to play .........
And they brought that to Havana.
The rhythm is son.
The son ....
Oh, I see.

The son. Now, now, when they brought that, on account that was black, they - was played among blacks, that type of music, like here, jazz among the new - among blacks - so they was good, you know, the people start to like because they were very rhythmic and very, very acceptable music; so in those days no club, no incorporated club will allow to play son in the - in the society.
It was banned?
- - - between the black - - - club they don't allow the sexteto to play; they were dancing the charanga or tipica - the one with bombardino and and figle and trumpet.
And bombardino - What is the American word for it? - or the English word. Is that a trombone?
It is noise between a - a trumpet and is - is a is a it has a range very in between a figle and a - a --
What kind of a instrument is a figle?
That was a metal thing, a metal thing.
Well, What did it sound like? Like a trumpet?
Like a trombone.
A trombone.
Like trombone.
I see. Okay. So then the music played, the popular music was more like for danzon bands or symphony bands, Right?
Ah - Hah
Why was the Afro-Cuban son - ah - overlooked? Was there a reason for it?, why they were ignored or wanted to be?

No, because the - they had so much black influence. In those days, there was the beginning of the Republic of Cuba and everybody want to run away to have anything or any mixture with blacks. Everybody want to be white, so......
Even the Afro-Cuban wanted to be white?
No, they.....
I am talking about the mulato that passed for white.
The mula--- the the half-breed, the one that it was lighter.....
He wanted to be white.

They want to be white so they refused to be, to accept, what the black people was doing. That was a second-rate, third-rate music. They don't want to be bothered. Charanga, it was almost a semi-classic thing. It come from the - they call it Charanga francesa, because the flute, the wood flute they was playing was originated in France and in England and it was a European instrument. That flute was used by the army to play a march to to create a gay atmosphere for the soldiers.
Macho, since you were one of the ones discriminated against, How did you feel? Tell me exactly what you felt when a country - when a country

Well, I have a different opinion about the the way - - I felt very bad because my grandfather was white and he was a gentleman and it was a legitimate - legitimate marriage, it was no flight-by-night; so I feel bad because my my grandfather was a gentleman and he treat my mother like a princess......
No, but you yourself and other Afro-Cubans, Were there any complexes because they were black and made to feel inferior because of a racist government that instilled this in the public mind?
Well, the most important thing is that the greatest warrior, the greatest guy in the Cuban independence, was black. Quintin Bandera, the whole family of Maceo, there was about five.......
Antonio Maceo?

The mother of Antonio Maceo, Jose Maceo, and two or three more Maceos, they died for the revolution. So when the ah - when the United States put the Main in the Habana harbor and blew up and I don't know if it was a accident or was a purpose to declare the war to Spain, because geographically or strategically United States need Cuba for the Panama, Canal de Panama, like Puerto Rico. They was looking for -'for protection. Geographically, Cuba and Puerto Rico was practically the backbone of the defense for the canal they were building.
Okay, I got the political picture now.
Now, Macho was a young kid, he went to school but he was concentrating on music. At that time, Macho, Were there any popular Afro-Cuban musicians that made Afro-Cubans feel very proud?
Oh, definitely. Tres Linda Cubanas, ah- ah- El Gallo Blanco de Maria, ah-- numerous of son montunos because that was the backbone of the thing; and then they start......
What about musicians or rumberos de la calle? Were there many?
Oh yeah! Tanganito, Malanga, Andrea Baro, Roncona; you name it.
What did they do, exactly?

Well, they was people like they was, let's say, they improvised. They was dancers, professional dancers in their own right; so they was so creative that in everyplace, because that was the only outlet we had, dance. Like when I came here I saw the Savoy, how many dances they create at the Savoy. Susie Q, Big Apple, Jitterbug, so forth, so on; so that's the only outlet we had in those years.
So a rumbero was a fellow that danced in the streets?
Not in the street, in private parties.
Oh, in private parties too?

They used to go to the what they call it, barracon, where the sugar mill workers used to sleep. They used to celebrate rumba so they got together. In those days, I remember my father had a grocery store in Guini, and Malanga
and Tanganito) they come to my father's grocery store and ask me for rice and beans and tasajo, you know, the parched meat. So I used to give it to them because I liked rumba, because I am black.

I like rumba and everything so they used to invite me. "Okay, Macho", they used to call me Macho, "Macho, okay, you are invited for so and so and so on; because I used to go Friday night to this particular place, like you say from here to Brentwood - that was the distance between Guini and Havana - so because my father want to, he want me to be acquainted with his business, he want me to follow his step, so I used to go out there Friday and come back Sunday to Havana to go to school Monday. So I enjoyed it tremendously. Saturday, that was a day! and Sunday in the daytime, forget it!
Okay. These jam sessions, the only thing I can think of calling them, they were African in origin, right? Were they taken from any religious cults? - the music - they used the sacred bata drum?

Well, let me tell you. Ah - to us - the Yoruba religion o Santeria o brujeria, whatever they call it, to us was like the Catholic religion or Protestant or Pentecostal or whatever. We create, we made an extract, we extract ours all those rhythms and we created what is the Cuban music now, what is Salsa, Mambo, Chachacha, Columbia, whatever.
So what you are saying then, from these religious cult music is where the Afro-Cuban, the Afro-Cuban root music came?
Right.
Right from those rumbas ah?
Right.
Okay. Do you know the names of the rumbas?
The roots?

Yes. Guaguanco, 'El Guaguanco Es Lo Mas Sublime que Cubita Creo,' that was written by Ignacio Pineiro, that now if he was alive he was about 105 years old, and Cotinzen, from another neighborhood, and Malanga - he was a good rumbero and a good composer - Roncona, he was a good composer too, and there was a numerous composers.
So all the popular Cuban rhythms today, what they call Salsa today, were taken from this cult music in Cuba I see.

Create by the Creole because the religious part we never used it, we never used the religious part because we respect, we was so close, because my grandmother was African and the other mother, so we just can't play around with the religion.
Okay. So the rumbas - El Palo, La Yuca, El Guaguanco and the rumba all came from this music.

El Palo is a - is a - is another religion that we say is not is not a Christian religion. Is something to ah, to ah, to do a lot of a lot of things; Voodoo is a Voodoo so Malanga and Yuca that was the name they did because that was the the what we eat, the yuca, malanga, you

know, they are like potatoes, so they used to name what we actually like to eat, like yuca, malanga, name, so you know how they apply such a number to a rumba - now they say yuca - so they use to create because the most popular thing that what happened in Cuba is that everytime that we created a type of number, we created a dance for. That's why it became popular.
I see.

That happened with Bossa Nova here. There was no dance and the people like to listen to a Bossa Nova, it is a beautiful thing, but it was no dance for that. It was not like a Samba and march and and whatever.
I see now that as a young, a young man growing up, you were very aware of your African roots. Were the other Afro-Cubans aware of it also?

Definetely. It was no way out. We was in the same neighborhood like a - ah - let's call it ghetto, where people just getting to be like a one-track mind, just enjoy themselves, get whatever is left.......
No, but what I am driving at Macho, is that all the young Afro-Cubans there were aware of Africa and their roots.
Oh, definitely.
The mother country, right?
Yes.
Were there any that didn't want to know about it and just wanted to say I am Cuban, I only want to know about what's happening here now.

There was just few, because in account of my time, my age, that was almost the beginning of the country and eawrybody was celebrating the freedom, helped by the United States, there is no question about it, otherwise we still been fighting in Cuba with the Spanish because it was a big country.
Uh - Huh

So that combination of the declaration of the war in America to Spain; Spain knew that they are going to lose with United States because the United States was so close. So they give up Cuba, they give up Puerto Rico and Philippines and so forth and so on. So everybody was so enthusiastic about the freedom and about and enjoying what we what was Spaniard because we respect all the property, everything that the Spanish has out there. I think it is the only country in the world that had freedom from one particular country and respects its property. We respect everything that they has.
I see. Macho, there came a time where your father moved to the cigar makers' projects in Pobolote and you met Mario Bauza. Tell me, how did that come about? What do you remember about that day?
Well, it was a beautiful thing.
How old were you?
I was about sixteen. Estela was about twelve and Mario was about fourteen. I am older than Mario two years; but Mario was an accomplished musician. He was playing with the Philharmonic.
At that time?
Oh yes, Mario he was graduated when he was eleven or twelve.
Had you been into music before meeting Mario?
Yes.
Okay, tell me.

Yes, so Mario had one of the best teachers in the country. He was a top ten clarinet player, Hugo Cien, and his godfather, Arturo Andrade, he was a musician in the - for the army - army band, a good musician, so in order he could kill time in Pabolote, he opened a school of music, free; so Mario used to sing by ear all the lessons, when he was seven, so he says: 'Oh yeah, you could sing by ear the lesson? - ah ------
You mean like Do - Re - Mi

Yeah, Do - Re - Mi - and Mario used to know practically the whole book of solfeggio or solfeggia and he forced Mario to read and make himself a musician where he start that he know really to to Hugo Cien and then he went to the Municipal Academy. Oh, as a matter of fact, about two or three months, he received all his - all his papers from the Academy of Music in Cuba.
Okay. Macho try to think back to that time where you first saw Mario and your sister introduced him. What do you remember about that? - that incident.
Well, on account that I was a music
lover and Mario was a well-educated, musically, so to me was a good - a good thing because he wasn't somebody that, you know, that you don't know where he is from. He was an accomplished musician.
You already knew of him before you met him?
Oh, yes.
You did.
I knew about it - Oh yes
You knew about him enough. Okay, so your sister says: "This is Mario Bauza". What happened after that?
Well, they start to, you know.....
Did you start hanging out together?
Yes, he my house, he used to come to my house and talk and this and this and that.
What, what did you talk about as young men?

Well, about six or seven months after Mario, my sister introduced me to Mario, I start working in Havana with Sexteto Redencion. So Mario was working at the Inglaterra Theatre; in those days there was, there wasn't no movie - movietone. It was a silent........
Silent movies.
Si., so he - they used to adapt the semi-classic or classic music to the - to the silent music.
I see, to the movie then.
To the movie then; so I was working with

a sextet, naturally, he was a different category musically, but he was my official brother-in-law, so we had a good relation. So we used to go together to the movies and we make a date to go to a ball game because his father was a manager of a professional ball team and we liked baseball, we liked boxing, so we used to have a tremendous relation.
Okay. What about the music, did you ever talk about music or play together? Like I notice you were into the more ah - - Afro-Cuban thing and Mario was into the classical thing.
In classical thing, but Mario used to play with Antonio Maria Romeu, with ah-- this fellow that died a few years ago, the flute player and........
Belizario Lopez?

Belizario Lopez. He played with everyone, even with the Tipica orchestra because they had two clarinets and trumpets and bombardino and figles and the symphonic timbales, and he was all over the place. He is, as a matter of fact is about six or seven months, the one that is in charge in Cuban culture, musical culture in Cuba, he was asking questions ah - - Mario about the Cuban music because Mario is older than him about twenty years.
How many instruments does Mario play?

Mario? He start playing piano, oh, no, clarinet and then he play piano, he could play bass, he plays trumpet, he plays flute, he plays saxophone, he is all around. But the most important thing about Mario is his conception, the analys, the the eh-- what he could make out of a little thing. He is like a science in music because is a lot of
people they read good music, they got good lip, they play good and everything, but they - what they play don't mean anything, but he could analyze a passage and make sounds like nobody else.
Uh Hum. Okay. When was the first time that you, that you and him played together?
Well - ah - in Cuba?
Yes.
We organized a band to go to Panama.
How old were you then?
I was about - about 17 or 18.
Okay, so that's about 1924-25, correct?
Right.
Okay. The Habanero, Bologna, all these sextetos are going strong now.
They were very strong.
Were they the inspiration for this?
Ahh - No, because what we had it was a combination that we had now in 1940. Panchito Riset was the singer.
Ah-Ha. You mean for that group that you and Mario formed?
Yeah, but he didn't appear in the picture because he was late, but I was playing guitar.....
What was the name of that group?
Ahhhh
Yeah, that was 1926, I remember the picture.
1926. Really, I don't remember, it was like a cooperative band.
I see. You were all young kids then, right?

Yeah. The only thing - the only older one was Arcelon Perez, that he lives in Mexico now, and Poligemo the bass player. The rest, Miguelito Valdes the violin --, he was about his early twanties, the rest was a bunch of young guys.
Okay. How many numbers did you have in your repertoire, in your book?
In that particular orquesta?
Yeah.....
Oh, we had about ten or fifteen.
Okay. Do you remember any of the names of the .....
Yeah. 'Manicero', naturally; we had 'Green Eyes,' we have Danzon that Antonio Maria Romeu give it to Mario, and we were helped practically everyone because Mario knew everyone.
Okay. Who were the vocalist on that group?
Panchito, Panchito Riset and myself.
Who sang the lead?
Panchito Riset.
Okay. And you sang second voice?
Yes.
And what part did Mario play in the group?
Mario was saxophone and clarinet.
Who was the leader of the group?
Mario
Mario was. Okay. Where did you work?

We worked - we was rehearsing at the a nightclub that was located where the - the owner of the nightclub was the owner of a radio station and he learned to, you know, that he want the room for rehearsal and we rehearsed about two three weeks waiting for the contract coming from Panama because we was with a group of dancers and we was the orchestra to play for them.
Did you ever get to go to Panama?
No.
What happened?
Well, one of those things, everything just failed.
I see. Okay. At that time your family is increasing, you - What were the other children now....
There was Estela, there was Graciel, there was Rogelio, Jr. and Martha.
Okay. Did any of them get the music influence . . .
Graciela And Estela.
Okay. What were they doing at that time when they were -------
At that time they went to - they was in school - they were younger than me, they was going to Hermanas Oblatas. That was an organization from New Orleans, black
nuns, that they opened that particular private school in Havana, Catholic school, by black nuns.
Okay, so Graciela and Estela went to the...
Estela and Anisa.
Alicia went to that school,
To that school.
And what were they, singing or learning an instrument? Or what?

I have the Pupi Campo arrangement, I have the recording and it's very, very good.
Yeah.
So that's how it came about.
And I wrote another number too, that I, what you call it, the, the ....
"Congo Mulence"?
"Congo Mulence"
Is in one of Tito Puente's album.
Uh - huh.
Yeah, 1968. Okay Macho, in 1959, no '58, you come out with another blockbuster called "Kenya", on Roulette.
Uh - Huh.
How did that come about?

Well, was a combination of Seijo, Mario, ah what you call it, ah the owner of Roulette, and to make another album because "Afro-Cuban Suite" was a success. As a matter of fact, they reissued it. And before we made "Flute to Boot", with ....
You made "Flute to Boot" after.
After.
Right, with Herbie Mann.
... with Herbie Mann.
Yeah, but you have "Kenya" there, you have Cannonball Adderley and a lot of jazz groups.
Yes.
Who got them all together?
Joe Newman - - Well, ahhh
Morris Levy?
Morris Levy ...
I see.
.... because Joe Newman was playing with Count Basie and Count Basie was signed with Roulette. So, it was a big family.
Okay, and how did you feel about the "Kenya" album?
Oh, very, very entuthiastic. The idea, just the idea to make another album, that was a beautiful thing.

"Afro-Cuban Suite" and "Kenya" are the best Afro-Cuban jazz album the Machito orchestra has recorded, you know. Ahh - 1959, you made "Mi Amigo Machito" and you made "La Feria de las Flores - A night with Machito", but on the "Mi Amigo Machito", you have "Israeli", I think, "Cha-Cha" ...
Yeah, yeah, "Israeli ....
... but you have "El As de la Rumba", How did you come by that number?
Well, that number is a Cuban composition, by a Cuban composer.
By Silvestre Mendez.
Yes, Silvestre Mendez; so we found a piano part and we give it to Renee and Renee made the arrangement and we recorded it.

Beautiful! because right now, today, that's one of your hottest numbers that nobody ever gets tired of listening to that, especially me. Ahh - so things slide by, we are into 1960-61. A trip to Japan materializes. How did that come about?
Well, there was a Colonel that was a fan of my band from way back to Charlie Parker and so forth, and he had in mind to bring the band up there. But, naturally,

the army had enough money to bring a band up there, so he submitted the idea to a nightclub owner and they got together and they send a letter to my booking office, Curbelo, Jose Curbelo, and they made the arrangement and we went to Japan and we spent three months up there. It was a success.

Okay, before you went to Japan, Macho, you were in Los Angeles, correct? You did two albums there, at the same time. You did The World's Greatest Latin Band and "Machito and the Crescendo". How did that recording come about? Did you go to California with the intent of doing those records?
No.
It just happened while you were there, right?
Yeah, we were there to make a tour of practically every town in, in ....
Before you left for Japan.
Ah - ha .....
Ah - ha

....and we was there working and the owner of the company come across with us and say: "Gee, I would like to record". We was free, we had finished with --- As a matter of fact, we was signed yet with Tico. We had to send a letter and have the permission for the recording and ----
That's right, because you were with Tico until 1965,'66.
... and he was very nice to allow us to make those ......
Mr. Levy?
Levy, yes. He sent a letter of permission to make those two albums.
Okay, from California you went to Japan?
No, we come back to New York ....
Uh - huh
... and then the thing just come about.
I see, but what did you do in New York before you went to Japan?
Oh, we was playing at the Birdland.
Appearing at Birdland?
Yes
Okay, in Japan now, what do you remember about that, the most significant thing of that trip?

Japan, to my humble opinion, is a first-class country. Very receptive, ahh very -- here they say polite, but I think they are that way because we wasn't there saving no life, we was playing music and they treat us like kings. Full of respect, very gracious to me about everything and we had a tremendous time.
Did they appreciate your tipico stuff or .....
Everything.
Everything, eh?
Everything.
Was it intended for you to stay there three months or is that .....
No, the contract, the contract lasts for three months.....
For three months ...
Yes
Okay --
... twelve weeks
... and did you play the same place all the time?
No, first we did a tour for the principal cities up there ...
Yes?
... and we played practically every industry, because in those areas, I don't know if they still do it, they used to work twenty-four hours, so every eight hours they had a concert.
You mean you went to a factory and played for ....
Yes.
... the employees?
They had auditorium, beautiful!! We had good sound and well-prepared the pianos, everything was ...
Were you the only North American band there in Japan at that time?
In that particular time, yes.
Yes, okay. Ahh did they have any Latin music recordings there?
Oh yes, Los Panchos, Los Panchos was ....
They liked Los Panchos?
Oh!! They was crazy about them.
Trio Los Panchos?
Yes.
Okay. What about on the radio? Did they ever play Latin music?
They was playing twenty-four hours, Latin music.
Latin music?
Yes.
Like, for instance, who?
Like for instance, Perez Prado was a big name up there. Ahh Cugat, it was a big name too, and then us after Tito Puente. He went up there, but we come back here ....
Yeah, because Mario went too ...
Yeah.
.... the same year and that. So then, would you say the Japanese people liked Latin-American music?
They love it.
What about in record stores, were there Latin-American records?
Yes, all over.
What about your stuff, was it there in records racks?
Yes, before we got there they had records that we recorded maybe five or six years.
Ahh!! On the Tico label?
Yes
Ah-Ha, okay. Macho, you came back, the Pachanga was hot then. What did it do to the band?
Well, we was working, not as much as I would like to because the Charanga wasn't, you know, very popular and ....
(Second side of last tape (IV) -- pause - then)
.... collector's items.. You are not satisfied with that song?

Yes, it was good, very good. To me was one of the best recording that we had, but is possible that we was kind of late. Is like for instance, you try to record a disco now. It's kind of late. Sometimes you don't move as fast as you should.
Isee, Isee.

And in many case too, you record with a company that take three or four months to release what you record because they looking for the time, for the numbers, and, 'no, this number is good for the spring, this number is good for the fall', whatever, and by the time you realize they -- When you release the number is old, everything is ...
Didn't you record a number called "Variedades"? Was it you or Tito Puente?
"Novedades" or "Variedades"?
Yeah, well no, did you put any Bop - Bossa-novas?
Yes, we played bossa-nova.

Okay, all right. I know you were having a difficult time getting work then, because most of the brass bands, not the flute and strings and rhythms orchestras, the brass bands, the big orchestras were having a hard time getting work. You decided to go to Puerto Rico then. What made you decide to go to Puerto Rico?
Well, see, what ....
I understand you were going to go and live there.
Uh- Huh
What year was this?
Ahhh
I know you came back in ....
.... Yes, in the last....
Yeah
Was Rene Hernandez still in the band when you went to Puerto Rico?
Yeah, yes, no, no ...
He already had left Tito Rodriguez ...
He left with Tito Rodriguez, yes.
Okay so then that was /66 then, okay. Now, tell me why did you want to go to Puerto Rico to live?
Well, first of all, sentimental reasons. My wife is from Puerto Rico and practically everything that I have done is based in a Puerto Rican atmosphere and I
have a tremendous response from the Puerto Ricans. If it wasn't for the Puerto Ricans, I won't be here, I won't even have a band.
Okay. You took your band down there, how many members went with you down there?
We had -- we cut the band because there was like a lounge like ....
OH!! You were playing down there then.
Yes
I see, okay ....
Yes
.... with the intention of staying there.

Ummnn - no, because I still have my children, they was in school time. My daughter was finished high-school, the other one went to college and so I , you know, sentimental reasons make you sacrifice a lot of things.
Okay, so you had ten men with you. How long did you stay there?
We spent up there eight months.
Eight months?
Eight.
You were practically living .... Was Mario Bauza and all the guys with you?
Yeah, everybody.
At that time.
My sister ....
What made you come back then, what made you not stay down there?
Ahhh - sentimental reasons. My ....
You didn't have no problems down there getting work?
No, no, no, not at all.
Okay, all right. So what made you decide to come back then?
My family.
I see.
My wife, her mother, the grandchildren; we start to getting into the grandchildren and things, and you know, so we had to come back.
When you came back, did you get work right away?
No, but in a month or so we was organizing. We was playing at the Casa Blanca, the Chez Jose, and, you know, ....
Yeah, the Chez Jose was popular at the time.
Yeah.
Now the bugaloo was reaching its peak then. First the pachanga hurt you, now you come back from Puerto Rico, the bugaloo is there, did that hurt you?
Right.
Okay. They were hiring the young kids' bands .... Right?
Uh-Huh
How did the band survive then?

Well, I always believe that something with quality always prevail. Ahh - you have a solid organization and people always respect the organization that is solid, that it give a good service; because we was a mature band. Not just because the people was an advanced age or whatever, is that we had the responsibility of a professional organization. We wasn't like young kids celebrating to play a dance because they are going to meet a lot of girls and nothing like that. We were doing that because we made living out of it. So our responsibility was different.
Well, because of the popularity of bugaloo, were you able to work as often as you would have liked to?

Listen, I don't recall very well, but we were doing all right playing three or four times a week, practically what we were doing before. Sometimes we might have two dates, but we were doing, considering ...
You were doing okay?
Yes
All right. Then what prompted you to record that bugaloo album for Cotique?
Because we signed with Cotique with George Goldner and then he was a good marketing man. He had that knack that he know what the people would like.
Did that album do anything for the band?

I don't know, I don't think nothing happened because he was more entuthiastic with the young ones and there was too many young guys in the company that we might create problem with the rest of the artists.
I see.
Not just jealousy, insecurity.

I see, okay. There's an album better than that one you did for Cotique. You did two years before that, when Martin Luther King had died, "Machito goes to Memphis". There was no promotion on that at all, Macho.
Well, we .....
You did that for RCA.

Yes. We was so lucky, because when that album start to, they start o spread out for the exhibition, the late Martin Luther King got killed and as mentioned, "Machito comes from Memphis", nobody want to know about Memphis. The people they was so ashamed. They lose a great guy like Martin Luther King, that he mean so well, that both groups they don't want to hear about Memphis, really. So now "Machito goes Memphis" so it wasn't called for for that particular time.
Uh-huh, but yet most of these albums finally went to other countries and they become best sellers there.
Right.
Were you aware of that?
Right.

Okay. Macho, in the seventies you are losing or you lost a lot of your men from the original band. You only had John Kins, Pin Madera and a few guys left. You had a lot of turnover in your band, you are getting a
lot of young jazz musicians which really enhanced the sound because they brought new ideas. Did you like it that way or would you've rather hold on to the older men.

Well, I always considered that a change is always, most of the time, for the best; and they was young musicians, very enthusiastic and with good qualifications and not just that it just was good qualifications, they listened to us. They listened to us about what we want and they was flexible enough to play close to what we want, so we was happy, really.

Okay. There are times when you have super sidemen like Chocolaté Armenteros, Jose Chombo Silva, Mario Rivera, Mauricio Smith, and I've heard the band when you didn't have them. They didn't sound as good, but it sounded very good, so you've proven one thing to me, that you always found somebody to fit in with your band. How are you able to do this?

Well, I, is a matter of experience, not that I know all the answers, but I know my music very well and the music is the arrangement that's top-flight because they are made by top-flight arrangers, so when everything is written right and you just read close to what is written, got the sound good.
Yeah, but how do they come out to phrase it the way you want it? Have you told these fellows? Have you instructed them how you want it done?
Oh, definitely. We play and there's a little thing here, there, that they might want to turn their way

and I say: listen, your way is beautiful and is perfect, but you see, this music you just cannot play like Charlie Parker because this is not Afro-Cuban jazz. This is tipico Cuban music. This got to be phrased different. The attack, the dynamics, all the things is completely different than to play jazz. Jazz has its way and this music has its way because this music has its roots and you have to respect the roots of this music like we respect the next one.
There's a phrasing and intonation that gives the Machito sound a unique sound. Do you teach it to these fellows?
Definitely.
All of them, all the new sidemen that come in.
Yes. No, we don't start playing until we get in tune ....
I see.
.... it's not that somebody come along from the street and put the mouthpiece and start playing. No, no, no.
Do you go -- How do you get these sidemen? Do you go looking for them or how do you select them?

Well, in many cases I went to places and listen to a fellow or recommend by somebody that is qualified to recommend a musician; like for instance, I have a trumpet player now and he recommend another trumpet player. I mean, if he is really a trumpet player, he is going to recommend the one as good as he.
How did you get Waymon ReId?

Well, because Waymon ReId liked good music and good book. Wayman ReId's been playing with the best bands including one of the finest, Count Ba^sie. So he know what we had in our group. He know that Chico O'Farrill arranged for us. Rene Hernandez people, they had arranged too, because he played Chico O'Farrill arrangement with Count Ba^sie. So he just - is something that you have to figure it out yourself.- Okay, I am going to play with such a band that had top-flight arrangement, I am going to enjoy it and I am going to be in company of so and so, and so and so, and so- because is a mouth to mouth thing.
Okay, did you and Mario always talked these things over or did one of you just go ahead and do it?
No, we talked over a few times, but it was a personal understanding.
Okay, you and Mario has always been like partners, right?
Absolutely.
Okay, and you never did anything without letting the other one know.
And even when he decide for something, it was for the best because he is a top qualified musician. So I had nothing to say for his decision, musically, because it was so well, so what should I say?
Okay. Macho, in 1969 you recorded "Solo Machito". You didn't record again until 1972, for Americana, then you didn't record again until 1976. These long absences
of recordings those years apart, does it hurt you, and does it hurt the band.
No, the thing is this. We kept working, not as much as we want to because .....
Is this because of the new recordings?

No, because who has the most exposure. The new generation know more. You just can't fight with the replacement, you just can't fight with exposure, so we - we had our problems. But the people that want to dance, they was dancing with my band, listen to the new one that had all the, I mean, radio exposure and they don't, I mean, expose all those things like second-rate and nothing like that. We was there with all the impact and, as a matter of fact, there wasn't no abuse like, you know, a guy that is punch-drunk or his reflex that's no good. His reflex was there.
I know you got over 200/ RPMs, way over 200. About how many albums would you say you got recorded?
Gee, I never keep track, really.

Okay, I know it runs into about fifty or around that area. Now, with all these recordings that are out there, why haven't disk jockeys played some of your recordings? You know, we have a lot of Latin music now, not enough Latin music on the air now, but more than we've had any other time before. We have Roger Dawson, we have - myself and Polito Vega are the only ones that are playing Machito recordings. Why haven't the other ones played them, Macho? Does it bother you?
No. Let me tell you, if they had the ....
I want to add that WKCR, Carlos de Leon, Jose Luis Morin and Cheo Diaz, play a lot of Machito records.

All right, those people, they know what they are playing, they like what they are playing. I don't like to somebody play my records because is in the program, because somebody forced them to play or for the administration say play Machito records. I like to listen to the music that the disk jockey wants to play. That made me enjoy more than if I know that's above the fifteen minutes, the twenty minutes or whatever, to listen to the music that I play or because the promoter, that's going to run the dance, in that particular segment of his advertisement include my number. I know that my number is included because I want to play that particular number.

I see. Okay, a lot of band leaders do not like people to record them live because they fear that a bootleg record is going to come out years later. Yet you have been one of the few, along with Jose Curbelo and Noro Morales, who were recorded live years ago at La Conga club, the China Doll and other places like that. The Band Box, La Bamba, and you did more live recordings which are now bootleg records and tapes out there. They have helped keep you alive and out there because WBAI and WKCR have played a lot of these things and the young generation has not heard them and they enjoy it with the stories attached to it. Now, because of this happening, don't you believe that you have benefited by this?
Definitely. Listen, whoever record our music

and play it over the radio or even play it in a party, they 're helping us, they're educating the people that are in the party or educating the people that listen to the radio station. Is no such a thing that you could have a diamond in the vault in the bank and the people will know that you have that three-karat diamond or whatever you have. You have to take a chance that somebody take it away from you and show the diamond.
Now that you've heard all those recordings that were taped-recorded without your knowledge like the ones with Howard McGhee and Brew Moore and Charlie Parker, are you glad that they were recorded?
Yes.
Why?

Because whoever - I am a sentimentalism, now, whoever record what I am playing is because he likes what he is hearing. So, they give you a great satisfaction and maybe an incentive to keep playing the best, the best way that is possible to play, because this is a message and is a communication. I consider that music, the one that I made or whoever made it, is a communication and is a happy communication.
Macho, wouldn't you also say that had someone not recorded these, these moments, these great moments of Latin music would've been lost?
Definitely.
Because here someone without your knowledge recorded it, now they have perpetuated Machito with
Charlie Parker live at the Royal Roost, Machito and Howard McGhee, Machito and Harry Belafonte, Machito with John Henry Lewis, of the Modern Jazz Quartet, ahh - Do you feel that it was a good thing?
Definitely.
What about - Are you going to fight for royalties for things like these?
Is foolish.
Why?

How could you keep control of this division in Thailand, how could you know if they sell your records in Finland? Well, now we are lucky that we went to Finland, but if I never had the chance to go to Finland, how are we know that it played my music or selling my records in Finland? As a matter of fact, in account of your broadcasting and your interview that you had sent to Finland, we had the opportunity to go out there and Tito Puente to go there in account of them.
Okay, so that did result from the live recordings that I made at the Corso. So then it has been effective.
Absolutely.
So then your advice to band leaders is, if someone wants to record you live, go ahead and do it...
No, no.
.... and not to worry about the royalties?
Well, listen, if you sell two thousand records, how much you going to get? Do you think that is possible to have the publicity that all those records - they, I mean

those numbers that they record and spread out or sell bootleg, whatever, you going to pay for that publicity? Is like a lot of people say: "Machito, could you go to a lots of benefit, so and so, and so and so", and maybe you are going to appear for one thousand people, doing something for a worthy cause. You are involved with something humanitarian. All those things is belong to an artist. Is an obligation to do, that the artist makes, or you are not an artist.
In other words, you believe record companies with all the publicity that you are getting, that they are entitled to keep the royalties because of the money they are laying out up front?

Well, I see many, many, many artists that on account of the publicity at the, the record company had provided, make millions of dollars. Millions, because you could sell one-hundred-thousand copies, spread out in, let's say, in two cities and you could work in those two cities two, three times a year. If you are going to call if for $100,000.00 of royalties, how much it will be?; few thousand dollars, and I see guys they have sold half a million records distribute the whole world and making a tour for a year, all through the world, doing special appearances. Do you think you have money enough to publicize your name without a recording in that company? Maybe I am wrong, maybe I don't know what I am talking about.
No, it's an outlook because if you feel that the companies are laying out money to promote you, then
they should get something in return. It's fair, it's fair. Okay, Macho, think back now. Forty years you've been a band leader, fifty years you've been in music, have you regretted anything?
No, if I had start all over again, as a matter of fact, I will retire when God tell me to retire.
Okay, let us say Machito is twenty years old, now would you do anything different?

Just, just a little different. I'd went to a conservatory to know what I am doing, to know what everybody is doing, because I consider education the simplification of life. A good education make you a better person because you understand better. Comprehension is more clear.
In other words, if you had your life to live over you'd make sure you get yourself a college education.
Oh, yes, no question about it. I don't want to miss the punch line of life.
Are you happy today?
Yes, very.
Are you satisfied with your band today?
Yes.
Is there anything else in life that you want to do?

Gee, I would like to see my grandchildren to have a good career and make something at it. I am lucky because one of my daughters she send my grandchildren to every school that you can think. I have a five years old

grandchildren learning how to play piano. As you know, in this tribute, my grandson is eight to nine years and he plays two, three numbers and he read and a musician like Mario has said: "this kid is going to be a good musician"...
Mario, your son.
... and yep -- no, Mario, my brother-in-law ..
I see.

.... and when he say something like when you was in that particular interview with Mario Bauza that he said: "What I have to say? You have to say everything is because you know what you taling about".
Mario, I mean, Macho, how old are you now?
Seventy.
Are you thinking about retiring?
No.
Okay. Thank you.
End of tape IV and of interview.
