segments.title: Copyright notice and interview header
segments.summary: IJS copyright warning and the title page: Machito interviewed by Max Salazar, May 1980.

segments.chapter: Opening and Havana childhood
segments.title: Birth date, parents, siblings and ancestry
segments.summary: Machito gives his birth (1908), his parents Martha and Rogelio, five siblings, and the African and Spanish ancestry of his grandparents.

segments.chapter: Opening and Havana childhood
segments.title: Early Havana childhood and the fire in the solar
segments.summary: He recalls happy Havana, his father selling water glasses, setting fire to the stock, and living in the Jesus Maria solar.

segments.chapter: Opening and Havana childhood
segments.title: Childhood games and the Johnson-Willard fight
segments.summary: His favorite games were baseball and boxing; his father took him to see Jack Johnson fight Jess Willard, and he describes the fight and the claim it was fixed.

segments.chapter: Opening and Havana childhood
segments.title: Life in the solar and father's grocery business
segments.summary: Description of the two-room home, the move across the street, and his father's prosperous import, grocery and street-vendor business.

segments.chapter: Opening and Havana childhood
segments.title: A musical house: singers and orchestras at his mother's birthday
segments.summary: Popular singers and orchestras such as Maria Teresa Vera, Floro Zorrilla and Antonio Maria Romeu played at family parties.

segments.chapter: Opening and Havana childhood
segments.title: Cuban presidents of his boyhood
segments.summary: He names the presidents Gomez, Zayas and Menocal and explains why independence generals became presidents.

segments.chapter: Opening and Havana childhood
segments.title: When he first felt discrimination in Cuba
segments.summary: His father's wealth shielded him until he started working with Maria Teresa at the Academia El Encanto, where musicians were kept from mixing with the clientele.

segments.chapter: Opening and Havana childhood
segments.title: Private school and dodging music school
segments.summary: He attended a private school with the Prio Socarras brothers and played truant from music lessons.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: Idols of his youth: flute players and the charanga
segments.summary: El Moro, Panchito and El Rubio were popular flutists; danzon played by charangas was the dominant music.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: How the son came to Havana and was kept from society clubs
segments.summary: He explains the son came from Oriente, spread after soldiers learned the tres in Santiago, and was barred from society clubs.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: The bombardino and figle in the tipica orchestra
segments.summary: Machito struggles to describe the bombardino and figle, which sound like a trombone.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: Why the son was looked down on
segments.summary: Because of its black influence, light-skinned Cubans rejected the son, while charanga was seen as semi-classical European music.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: Feelings about racism; black heroes of Cuban independence
segments.summary: Machito answers about inferiority complexes by citing Maceo and Bandera, and gives his view of the Maine and US interest in Cuba.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: Rumberos and Afro-Cuban pride
segments.summary: He names rumberos like Tanganito and Malanga as creative dancers, comparing them to Savoy dances in New York.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: Weekends at the rumba barracon in Guini
segments.summary: He gave rice and tasajo to rumberos at his father's Guini store and was invited to their rumbas.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: Santeria and the roots of Cuban music
segments.summary: He says the Yoruba religion was to them like any church, and from its rhythms came mambo, salsa and cha-cha-cha.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: Rumba names, composers and the dances behind them
segments.summary: He names guaguanco composers, explains yuca and malanga rumba names, and says Cuban numbers always came with a dance, unlike bossa nova.

segments.chapter: Race, son and Afro-Cuban roots
segments.title: Awareness of African roots and Cuban freedom
segments.summary: Young Afro-Cubans were aware of Africa; he talks about enthusiasm for freedom after the war with Spain.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Meeting Mario Bauza and his musical training
segments.summary: Machito met Mario at Pobolote through his sister Estela; Mario was a trained clarinetist taught by Hugo Cien and Arturo Andrade.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Friendship with Mario; Sexteto Redencion and silent-movie theatre
segments.summary: They became friends, Machito joined Sexteto Redencion while Mario worked at the Inglaterra Theatre accompanying silent films.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Mario's range and musical mind
segments.summary: Mario played with Romeu and Belizario Lopez, many instruments, and Machito admires his analytical conception.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: The cooperative band for Panama that never went
segments.summary: Machito and Mario formed a band with Panchito Riset, Miguelito Valdes and others, rehearsed, but the Panama contract failed.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: His sisters' schooling and meeting Cachao
segments.summary: His sisters attended a school run by black nuns, and he describes meeting young Cachao and the musical Lopez family.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Why Afro-Cuban families chose music
segments.summary: Machito says music was a way out, comparing black entertainers in the US before publishers and white bands took control.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Joining Maria Teresa Vera's septeto as maraca player
segments.summary: After 1926 Mario worked at casinos while Machito played maracas with Maria Teresa Vera; he got the job through Miguelito Garcia.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Being fired by Maria Teresa Vera
segments.summary: After two years Vera dismissed him because he rehearsed with a radio quartet and she thought he would quit.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Playing with Sexteto Agabama
segments.summary: He joined Barroso's Agabama with Cheo Marquetti and Felix Chapotin, playing son montuno, which he says is now called salsa.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Musicians and women at dances
segments.summary: Dancers might meet women after the dance but musicians who did were fired.

segments.chapter: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
segments.title: Discrimination at the Spanish regional centers
segments.summary: Black clubs had no problem, but the Centro Gallego and Centro Asturiano were white Spanish organizations that pressured black musicians.

segments.chapter: Race and ethnicity in Cuba
segments.title: Chinese immigrants and Afro-Cubans in Cuban society
segments.summary: Salazar asks about Italians, Chinese, Haitians and Jews; Machito says all discriminated, the Chinese included, and that Chinese were brought in for menial jobs.

segments.chapter: Race and ethnicity in Cuba
segments.title: Chinese slurs, cooperative businesses and neighborhood ties
segments.summary: He explains the slur "ha quay", the reserved Chinese cooperative businesses, and how they depended on black neighborhoods.

segments.chapter: Race and ethnicity in Cuba
segments.title: Haitians and Afro-Cubans
segments.summary: Haitians came to cut cane and return home; Machito says minor trades were left to blacks and compares to Jewish holidays in New York.

segments.chapter: Race and ethnicity in Cuba
segments.title: Orientals in Cuban music; Mario Bauza's teacher
segments.summary: No Chinese-Cubans took up music except Mario Bauza's teacher, whose father was Chinese.

segments.chapter: Race and ethnicity in Cuba
segments.title: Why Afro-Cubans chose music while whites chose other careers
segments.summary: Machito says education was open to all but poor blacks doubted careers; white Cuban musicians like Moises Simons had conservatory chances.

segments.chapter: Race and ethnicity in Cuba
segments.title: Chinese into restaurants, laundries and groceries
segments.summary: The Chinese went into business, taking over grocery stores that Spaniards' children gave up.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Why Mario Bauza left Cuba in 1930
segments.summary: Mario, disillusioned when lesser white musicians took his jobs, left for New York as did Socarras, Lico Jimenez and Rico, as talking pictures ended jobs for black players.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Hearing Arsenio Rodriguez in 1933
segments.summary: Machito says Agabama and the Sexteto Bologna were far more advanced than Arsenio, who wrote music within his limits.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Mambo versus son montuno
segments.summary: Machito denies Arsenio created the mambo and compares son montuno to rhythm and blues versus rock and roll.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Arsenio's style compared with Machito's groups
segments.summary: Machito calls Arsenio unpolished but with flavor and fully black, while his own sextets were a half-breed music.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Leaving Agabama to run his father's beach restaurant
segments.summary: After Agabama (1933-36) he quit to work with his father's restaurant at a beach.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Sexteto Nacional and Alfredito Valdes
segments.summary: Clarifying dates, he explains he replaced a maraca player at Sexteto Nacional, then moved to Maria Teresa and then Agabama, and talks of Alfredito Valdes.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Agabama's repertoire
segments.summary: With Agabama he was second voice and maraca player; they played guarachas, guajiras and son montuno in a more advanced style.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: A musician's day, pay and chaperoned dances
segments.summary: He earned $3.33 a date, played eight to one every day, and dances were attended by women with chaperones under high moral standards.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Machado, the 1933 revolution and Batista's rise
segments.summary: Machito explains the Machado era, why Machado fell in August 1933, how sergeant Batista took control of the army, and Desi Arnaz's father as mayor.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Why he left Agabama in 1936
segments.summary: Dissatisfied as danzonete and charangas took over, he quit the sextet to work for his father; the Lopez-Barroso charanga is described.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Miguelito Valdes and Chano Pozo
segments.summary: Machito knew Miguelito Valdes and his family from childhood and says Chano Pozo came later and was younger.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Managing his father's restaurant at Biriato Beach
segments.summary: His father ran an open-air restaurant near the Casino Nacional in Marianao, with Machito as administrator.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Miguelito Valdes as bass player
segments.summary: While out of music for seven or eight months, Machito recalls Miguelito Valdes reorganizing a group and playing bass.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: Saving money to come to the United States
segments.summary: He saved quarters in an oil can, spurred by Mario's marriage to Estela and love of New York, and left despite his family's objections.

segments.chapter: Agabama, Arsenio and leaving Cuba
segments.title: The voyage on the SS Oriente
segments.summary: A hurricane stretched the trip to six days; he made friends among the merchant marines.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Arrival in New York and the Savoy
segments.summary: He stayed with his sister Estela and went nightly to the Savoy to hear Chick Webb, where Mario was rehearsing the band.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Working with Mulato's Three Habaneros at the Mella Club
segments.summary: He returned to music with Mulato at the Mella Club in Harlem, then a trip to Detroit.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: First recordings with Cuarteto Caney, Cugat and Noro Morales
segments.summary: Alfredito Valdes gave him his first recording break with Cuarteto Caney; he freelanced with Noro Morales, Cugat and Augusto Coen and played in Orquesta Siboney.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: The audition at La Conga and the blown fuse
segments.summary: Machito and Mario formed a band to audition at La Conga but the lights went out and a rival bandleader got the job.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Joining Orquesta Siboney under Alberto Iznaga
segments.summary: After Mario joined Cab Calloway, Machito stayed about a year with La Siboney and recorded with them.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Mario leaves Calloway to join Machito's band
segments.summary: Mario cabled that he was tired of the road, and they agreed to split the expenses; his arranger contacts helped the band.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Personnel of the band at the Great White Way
segments.summary: The small band had one trumpet, two saxes, timbales, bass and piano, mostly from Siboney.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Forming the Afro-Cubans at home with Mario
segments.summary: They planned the band in the house they shared, with Mario as musical director.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Mario's concept: a new sound with jazz-level intonation
segments.summary: Machito says their style had better phrasing and intonation because Mario had perfect pitch and wrote only what each musician could play.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Hiring jazz arranger John Bartee; Mario as musician of musicians
segments.summary: Mario hired jazz arrangers like Bartee, who loved Debussy, to bring legato lines and counterpoint into an Afro-Cuban band.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: How the band became Machito and his Afro-Cubans
segments.summary: Machito says the name was chosen by the club owner, not by him or Mario, replacing the Cuban New Yorkers name.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Original personnel of the Afro-Cubans
segments.summary: Trumpets Doc Cheatham and Mario, saxes Johnny Nieto, Freddy Skerritt and Pin Madera, with Tony Escollies, Bilingue, Julio Andino and Frank Ayala.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: First rehearsal at Father Divine's hall
segments.summary: They rehearsed in overcoats in an unheated hall at 122nd Street and 7th Avenue, for fifty cents an hour.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Early repertoire and arranger Pin Madera
segments.summary: The first book included El Muerto se fue de Rumba and Chacumbele; Pin Madera was the first arranger.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Approaching the Park Plaza: Montecino's guerrilla jibe
segments.summary: Machito asked the Park Plaza owner for a date and Montecino, whose dance was postponed, sneered at his guerrilla.

segments.chapter: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
segments.title: Top billing trick and taking over the Park Plaza
segments.summary: Machito put his name on top of the bill, won the crowd, and when Montecino left for another job, the band got the Park Plaza.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Mario and Machito as their own promoters
segments.summary: They booked their own dances, advertised on radio, and drew on the Puerto Rican colony of El Barrio.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Diosa Costello and Jack Robbins open doors
segments.summary: Diosa Costello brought publisher Jack Robbins, who introduced them to manager Jack Leer, and she recommended them to the Chateau Madrid.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Chateau Madrid, La Conga and the Beachcomber
segments.summary: They won over the Chateau Madrid, filled in for Sacasas at La Conga, and played the Beachcomber.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Meeting Hilda at the Park Plaza
segments.summary: After a Stork Club conga-line fundraiser, Machito met Hilda at the Park Plaza and bought her a Coca-Cola.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: First date at the Apollo and courting Hilda
segments.summary: Hilda took him to the Apollo to see Duke Ellington, then he tracked down her mother's home and they courted.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Their wedding
segments.summary: They married at City Hall, then in a Protestant church and finally the Catholic church for the children's schools.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: The apartment on East 111th Street
segments.summary: Machito describes their ground-floor apartment next to the firehouse.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Writing "Sopa de Pichon"
segments.summary: He improvised the tune at the Park Plaza over a vamp from Frank Ayala, naming neighborhood tough guys in the lyrics.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Writing "Paella"
segments.summary: Insulted when promoter Federico Pagani asked if he had tried paella, he wrote the tune on the subway.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Other compositions
segments.summary: Mambo a la Savoy with Walter Fuller and others; he estimates over 150 tunes.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Desi Arnaz's rise with Diosa Costello
segments.summary: Desi Arnaz became popular teaming with Costello in the Broadway show Too Many Girls and its film.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: Babalu: Miguelito Valdes versus Desi Arnaz
segments.summary: Miguelito recorded Babalu first but Arnaz's publicity made it his; Machito says Miguelito was unbothered.

segments.chapter: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
segments.title: La Conga in 1942 and how Tito Puente joined
segments.summary: Puente, a teenager, played with Siboney, was recommended by Mario to Sacasas, then joined Machito for a year and a half.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: World War II draft takes his musicians
segments.summary: The draft took band members; Pin Madera left first and was replaced by the Filipino Amado Punzalan.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Hiring flexible jazz players instead of Latin musicians
segments.summary: Machito says they picked adaptable American musicians who could be molded in phrasing rather than Latin players set in their ways.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Recording 26 tunes with Miguelito Valdes during the 1942 strike
segments.summary: Miguelito's first solo job was at La Conga with Machito; during the strike they recorded 26 sides in two days with little pressure.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Why the Decca tunes had already been recorded with Cugat
segments.summary: The numbers were little-known Cuban publications, and restrictions made repeat recordings hard.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Release and sales of the Decca 78 albums
segments.summary: The producer Perez had pre-sold 25-30 thousand copies in Latin America; albums of eight sides sold for about four dollars.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Live broadcasts from La Conga and the theme "Nague"
segments.summary: The band began broadcasting in 1942, opening with "Nague" in a John Bartee arrangement.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: How "Tanga" came about
segments.summary: Machito says Mario was wrong that he was there; "Tanga" grew from a vamp behind Miguelito's "Botellero" by pianist Varona and Mario's melody.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Draft notice and induction at Camp Upton
segments.summary: He worked fifteen days after the March notice, then reported to Whitehall Street and Camp Upton.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Jack Robbins and the coast-to-coast midnight broadcasts
segments.summary: Publisher Jack Robbins arranged radio time from La Conga to plug the music he published; few air checks survive.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Replacing Noro Morales at the China Doll
segments.summary: When La Conga became the China Doll, Machito's band filled in two weeks for Noro Morales.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Decca sessions of 1942 and the hit "Paella"
segments.summary: Perez of Decca liked "Sopa de Pichon" and "Paella"; well-rehearsed, they cut their records at the Decca studios without overtime.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Jack Robbins's file of rejected Latin numbers
segments.summary: The tunes recorded were Robbins stock numbers marked no good by Latin bandleaders; Mario's arrangements made them hits.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Marcelino Guerra brought to New York
segments.summary: Mario recommended Guerra, top composer in Cuba then singing with Arsenio Rodriguez, to Robbins; Machito compares him to Lecuona.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Plans for Marcelino Guerra and Varona's unreliability
segments.summary: From the army Machito said to put Guerra in his place; Mario formed Guerra's group, called the Second Afro-Cubans.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Piano chair: Varona, Joe Loco and Jose Curbelo
segments.summary: Frank Ayala left for the army, Varona was unreliable, and Jose Curbelo often sat in; Mario helped Curbelo start his own band.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Why the Second Afro-Cubans was formed
segments.summary: Mario wanted to give the talented Guerra a band for the off days, and Machito sang with him to help him get known.

segments.chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
segments.title: Promoting Saturday dances uptown
segments.summary: With no clubs, Machito, Mario and Federico Pagani rented ballrooms and kept bar receipts; Machito was king uptown.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Rivalry with Marcelino Guerra and battles of music
segments.summary: No heated rivals at first; people compared him to Guerra's swinging band, and they played joint dances that Machito promoted.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Back from the army: Jose Curbelo starts his band at La Conga
segments.summary: On discharge Machito returned to La Conga, where Curbelo had become a bandleader with a similar instrumentation but a different style.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Why no performance is the same
segments.summary: Machito says his band is no machine; "La Paella" played twice would come out differently depending on atmosphere and mood.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: The 1944 recording ban and studio pay
segments.summary: The Petrillo strike kept them from recording; studio pay was thirty dollars for four numbers on two tracks.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Sequence of record labels after Decca
segments.summary: After Decca he recorded for Continental, Verne, Mercury, Columbia under Mitch Miller, and later Tico.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: "Saludos Amigos" armed forces broadcast recordings
segments.summary: They recorded forty or fifty shows for the army at La Conga, a studio and the Palladium, with four-hour sessions; he also mentions Muzak.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Signing with Verne Records and the Rapping Day name
segments.summary: Cuevas's Verne label recorded Miguelito, Guerra, Trio San Juan and Machito; Guerra's Rapping Day was a pseudonym.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Duets with Miguelito Valdes and "Tierra va a temblar"
segments.summary: Machito explains the key change for Miguelito's singing and how Miguelito learned the arrangement in a day.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Why the Verne contract ended
segments.summary: Verne's owner wanted a catalog but had no distribution; Machito was released and went to Mercury.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Passing as Cubans in Miami
segments.summary: Billed as imported from Cuba, the mixed band avoided Florida segregation and Machito posed as interpreter for American-born Leslie Johnakins.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Treatment in Miami Beach
segments.summary: They were well treated, invited to see Walter Winchell, because Cubans were not considered black.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: A week-long trip to Havana during the Miami engagement
segments.summary: Because of ice-show renovations, he took Andino and Ubaldo Nieto to Havana while Mario saw his family.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Meeting Chano Pozo in Havana
segments.summary: He knew Chano Pozo from the CMQ and Cadena Azul stations.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Adding the conga to the band
segments.summary: The Miami band had Vidal Bolado on conga from late 1944; Machito says the conga is the second bass of the rhythm section.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Who Dizzy Gillespie heard: Mangual, Vidal and Chano Pozo
segments.summary: Machito says Dizzy never heard Bilingue; Chano Pozo impressed because he played between bass and drum without conflict.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: First New York band to use the conga permanently
segments.summary: Cab Calloway used it on records, Cugat used it more permanently thanks to Miguelito Valdes.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Percussionists: Bilingue, Chino Pozo, Escollies and Tito Puente
segments.summary: Machito sorts out the rhythm section: Escollies on timbales, Bilingue briefly, Chino Pozo on bongo, and Puente as timbalero and drummer.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Chino Pozo and Tito Puente leave with Jack Cole
segments.summary: Both left with dancer Jack Cole for $200 a week; Puente returned and was later drafted, while Chino Pozo went with Graciela.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Tito Puente as a young musician
segments.summary: Machito praises Puente as talented, always on time, ambitious and dedicated, already known to Curbelo.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Club Brazil engagement in California
segments.summary: After Miami the band went to Hollywood's Club Brazil in January 1946 and was a success with a well-rehearsed, young band.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Rene Hernandez, arranger from Cuba
segments.summary: Rene Hernandez changed the band, arranging with an authentic Cuban feel for Julio Cuevas and others.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Rene Hernandez's background in Cienfuegos
segments.summary: Rene came from Cienfuegos like Marcelino Guerra, was a gifted barber from a musical family.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Bringing Rene Hernandez from Cuba
segments.summary: With the army taking pianists, Curbelo's father recommended Rene; Machito's sister contacted him and he joined the union and Mario's household.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Three months in Los Angeles at the Club Brazil
segments.summary: They lived in Los Angeles while the club was in Chinatown, popular after Panchito Riset, and the show was broadcast.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Sightseeing, Desi Arnaz's studio and Los Angeles Latin bands
segments.summary: Machito toured Hollywood with Desi Arnaz and notes Eddie Cano's commercial combo as the other Latin band.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Dagan and discovering Olga San Juan for the Copacabana
segments.summary: Manager Dagan wanted a lead for the Copacabana chorus, and Machito recommended young Olga San Juan, whom a scout then hired.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Screen test at Columbia for Miguelito and Olga San Juan
segments.summary: Miguelito Valdes and Olga San Juan did a Columbia test with Machito's band; Olga made it, Miguelito didn't.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Teaching Betty Riley and the Music Craft album with Miguelito
segments.summary: Machito taught Betty Riley to sing Miguelito's numbers, then in California they backed Miguelito on a Music Craft album arranged by Rene.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Betty Riley insists on making the film with Machito's black band
segments.summary: Studio objected to a white girl with a black band, but she insisted on Machito because he played the real thing.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Making the film at Columbia and the Club Brazil routine
segments.summary: The short was filmed at Columbia in New York; in Los Angeles they played only the Club Brazil, six days a week for three months.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Hollywood visitors at the Club Brazil
segments.summary: Olga San Juan brought Carmen Miranda, Bing Crosby, Rafael Mendez and studio musicians, who marveled at the interpretation.

segments.chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
segments.title: Last days in Los Angeles; Pagani's publicity and "El Bongo Arrollador"
segments.summary: Federico Pagani handled publicity and set up twenty or so live broadcasts; they recorded the Bongo number with Verne.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Chano Pozo's first night at La Conga
segments.summary: Chano arrived in May 1946 recovering from a gunshot wound, and could not dance, so he did a barber routine around Pepe Beque.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Miguelito introduces Chano; Cachao and Pepe Beque hired as dancers
segments.summary: Miguelito introduced the Blen Blen composer, the crowd went wild, and Cachao and Pepe Beque were hired to dance nightly.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Mario introduces Chano to Dizzy; Miguelito's help
segments.summary: A couple of months later Mario introduced Chano to Dizzy, and Miguelito helped Chano a lot.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Recording Olga Guillot at Nola Studios
segments.summary: The band backed Olga Guillot on twelve numbers, arranged by Rene Hernandez, for a few bottles of liquor; Chano may have played conga.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Chano Pozo leads a percussion jam
segments.summary: At the Nola session Chano organized congas, bongos and timbales and showed his command of the style.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Coda recordings under Rene Hernandez's name; "Killer Joe" and "No Noise"
segments.summary: Verne-contracted, the band recorded for Coda as the Rene Hernandez orchestra; John Bartee wrote "No Noise" from his baby's crying.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Fred Robbins and Latin music on radio
segments.summary: Disc jockey Fred Robbins played the instrumental "Killer Joe" because he could not play Spanish vocals to his jazz audience.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Fred Robbins and the Town Hall concert
segments.summary: Robbins, enamored of Miguelito's showmanship, emceed and publicized the Town Hall concert that introduced Afro-Cuban jazz.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Reaction to Afro-Cuban jazz and the Carnegie Hall date
segments.summary: Audiences raved about the polyrhythm of conga, bongo and timbales, then Carnegie Hall followed with Sonny Stitt replacing Charlie Parker.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: The Town Hall evening: two shows and a mixed crowd
segments.summary: They played two 45-minute shows including typical music, to a mixed crowd of Latins and Americans who danced Latin music.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Tico Tico dances at the Manhattan Center with rival bands
segments.summary: Joint dance nights at the Manhattan Center had four bands including Noro Morales and Marcelino Guerra, and the crowds went wild.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: No rivalry with Noro Morales and Marcelino Guerra
segments.summary: Machito says mature bandleaders with settled styles did not feel rivalry, unlike Puente and Rodriguez, and that there were fewer bands then.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Publicity after Town Hall
segments.summary: Success spread by word of mouth; he says with the publicity of today's stars he would have been a millionaire.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Stan Kenton's tribute tune and "The Peanut Vendor"
segments.summary: Kenton recorded "Machito" after the concert; Machito's rhythm section then played on Kenton's "Peanut Vendor" at Capitol, working in harmony with drummer Shelly Manne.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Recording for Verne, Coda, Muzak and Mercury in 1947
segments.summary: He was recording steadily under several names, using numbers from Antobal's publishing house, Robbins, Chano and Guerra, plus Muzak instrumentals.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Never a record collector
segments.summary: Machito says he kept few of his records because his children and friends gave them away and he never thought of himself as a genius.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Playing the Apollo and Savoy Ballroom for black audiences
segments.summary: They played the Savoy twenty-five or thirty times; 95 percent of the audience was black, and danced the Afro-Cuban rhythm well.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Leaving Verne and recording for Continental
segments.summary: After Verne he recorded about 24 numbers for Continental, which had better distribution abroad; they heard the records in Japan in 1962.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Why Continental and Columbia dropped Latin artists
segments.summary: American companies lacked patience; there were hardly two Latin radio stations in New York, so records were not exposed.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Norman Granz brings Charlie Parker to record with the band
segments.summary: Granz, linked to Chico O'Farrill, heard the band at Birdland and the Palladium and wanted Parker to record "El Manicero".

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Flip Phillips versus Charlie Parker as soloists
segments.summary: Machito says Flip Phillips was more flexible, while Parker was an intellectual in chords and creativity.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Meeting Charlie Parker at the Palladium rehearsal
segments.summary: Parker listened to "Mango Mangue" twice and played the whole arrangement as if he had known it for years.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Granz picks the tunes; the arrangements were already existing
segments.summary: Granz selected pieces from arrangements the band had for a year, and Parker just played over them.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Parker and Flip Phillips compared as colleagues
segments.summary: Flip was Granz's favorite for being prompt and easy-going; Parker was unpredictable but never late for Machito's sessions.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Parker's frustration and the Carnegie Hall replacement story
segments.summary: After "No Noise", Granz was always looking for replacements; Machito explains Parker's frustration at being tolerated rather than accepted.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Working with Parker: no problems, always blaming himself
segments.summary: Parker played on top of the band, catered to them, and always said he could do better.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Parker sitting in at the Royal Roost; the "Asia Minor" bootleg
segments.summary: Parker came as a visitor and played with them; Salazar tells Machito of a bootleg recording of "Asia Minor" from the Royal Roost.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: George Shearing and Art Tatum
segments.summary: Machito shared two pleasant weeks at Birdland with Shearing, who credited him with his love of Afro-Cuban music.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Perez Prado's mambo versus his own arrangers
segments.summary: Machito says the mambo was nothing new, Prado aimed at a mass American audience, and his arrangers were more advanced.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Rhythms of "Babarabatiri", "Vaya Nina" and "Asia Minor"
segments.summary: He calls these records Afro-Cuban jazz and disliked the double-mambo tempo change on "Asia Minor".

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Why the mambo overtook Afro-Cuban jazz
segments.summary: Machito says mambo spread because American dance teachers made a dance for it, and anything danceable beat music to listen to.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Influence on Kenton, Les Brown, Woody Herman and Johnny Richards
segments.summary: Machito accepts that others borrowed from the band, but stresses Afro-Cuban jazz was a group creation by Mario and jazz players.

segments.chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Carnegie Hall, February 1949: "The Jazz Scene" concert
segments.summary: He recalls playing Tanga at Carnegie Hall with Ellington, Parker and Lester Young; the band's soloists made poetry from one chord.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Sonny Stitt sits in at Carnegie Hall when Parker is absent
segments.summary: Parker failed to appear for the Carnegie date, Norman Granz vouched for the young Sonny Stitt, who played "Tanga" and a second tune with the band.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: How "Asia Minor" was arranged and completed
segments.summary: The composer brought an arrangement lacking the right clave meter and bass syncopation; Rene, Mario, Machito and Bobby Rodriguez supplied the missing notes.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: The competitive hit year of 1949
segments.summary: Asked about the many mambo hits of 1949, Machito says other bands' success was good for the music and rivalry is egotism.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Playing Afro-Cuban jazz and tipica without conflict
segments.summary: Machito says Afro-Cuban jazz opened a new market without hurting tipica fans; both were played, sometimes in the same dance, on clave.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Mercury foxtrot-tempo records like "Call of the Mambo King"
segments.summary: Companies made them guinea pigs, simplifying with familiar melodies like "Donkey Serenade" over Cuban rhythm, and the records sold.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: How the Machito band came to open the Palladium
segments.summary: The Alma Dance Studios turned Palladium were failing; Machito, asking if the owner was prejudiced, proposed mixing audiences in a segregated era.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Subway dances and the Blen Blen Club
segments.summary: With Federico Pagani he handed out ten thousand flyers in subway stations, and with Chano Pozo's permission started the Blen Blen Club matinee with several bands.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Steady work at the Palladium; Tito Puente's Picadilly Boys
segments.summary: The band stayed fourteen to twenty weeks; discharged from the navy, Puente organized a group for a five o'clock matinee.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Ballrooms of the forties and the three bands
segments.summary: Few Latin bands were as versatile; Tito Puente and Tito Rodriguez later joined him at the Palladium.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Cubop City and the Royal Roost
segments.summary: The club above Jack Dempsey's opened with Artie Shaw and Machito, with Symphony Sid broadcasting from the Roost and Club Clique, later Birdland.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Howard McGhee and Brew Moore on "Cubop City"
segments.summary: Machito says Roost label partners Teddy Reig, Morris Levy and Symphony Sid paired McGhee and Moore against the complicated rhythm.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Impact of "Cubop City" and playing both crowds
segments.summary: Salazar says hearing it in North Carolina made him homesick; Machito says it brought jazz and dance dates in many cities with both audiences.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Naming "Cubop City" and who arranged it
segments.summary: Teddy Reig and Symphony Sid asked for a new "Tanga"; Mario titled it and Rene Hernandez arranged it, with McGhee and Moore filling in.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Among the first to play Birdland
segments.summary: Machito's orchestra was among the first Latin band at Birdland, played twenty times for Morris Levy, in late 1949 around the Afro-Cuban Suite.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Moving from Mercury to Columbia with Mitch Miller
segments.summary: Mitch Miller took them to Columbia's international department, where they recorded "Hobo Mambo" produced by Percy Faith.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Live-audience recording at the church on 30th Street
segments.summary: For "Frisilandia" and "Zambia" they brought seventy or eighty high-school kids and Palladium regulars to give audience atmosphere.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Why the band was not hired at the Palladium in the early fifties
segments.summary: Machito says three bands were too costly for the Palladium and compares with the high cost of touring now.

segments.chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
segments.title: Radio exposure and the Tico label
segments.summary: Salazar says DJs played only Tico records; Machito says rivals had better publicity men and compares it to sitting on the bench.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Accepting the music business and rotating favorites
segments.summary: Machito says he waited his time, calls it business, and notes that records fall from the charts as the industry rotates favorites.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Tito Puente demands top billing over Machito
segments.summary: Puente's hit year of 1952 won him top billing even at the Malibu; Machito accepted for his family and compares himself to Joe Louis.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Sizing up Puente and Tito Rodriguez
segments.summary: Both were good friends and talented; he did not mind because they played his music, and he saw himself as the champion playing challenger.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Slipping from No. 1: new personalities and three different bands
segments.summary: Salazar suggests the billing rivalry hurt; Machito says audiences like new personalities, compares Glenn Miller and boxers, and says his band was the architect.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: The "Mambo U.S.A." tour with Joe Loco
segments.summary: Conceived by George Gomez to promote Tico records, it gave a good contract and exposure; Puente joined, Tito Rodriguez never did.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Batista's 1957 reunion of Cuban musicians in Havana
segments.summary: Machito flew with Tito Puente, whom he and Mario had pushed to attend, to a two-week gathering of Cuban musicians.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Reunion in Havana: old friends, the ceremony and the medal
segments.summary: He met Bola de Nieve, Miguelito Valdes, Gilberto Valdes, Cachao, Arcano and Arsenio Rodriguez, and was honored at City Hall.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Writing "Bailen cha cha y guaguanco" on the plane
segments.summary: Fellove doubted Americans danced Cuban rhythms, so Machito wrote a tune on the plane home, recorded on the Tico album.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: How "Pilarena" and "Congo Mulence" were written
segments.summary: He wrote "Pilarena" at the Palladium after a girl from Pinar del Rio; Nilo Curbelo wrote it out and Puente arranged it for Pupi Campo.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: "Kenya" on Roulette
segments.summary: Roulette's Morris Levy and Joe Newman helped assemble Cannonball Adderley and other jazz stars after "Afro-Cuban Suite" succeeded.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: "Mi Amigo Machito" and "El As de la Rumba"
segments.summary: Rene Hernandez arranged "El As de la Rumba," a Silvestre Mendez piece, for the 1959 album.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: How the Japan tour came about
segments.summary: A colonel who was a fan arranged with a nightclub owner to bring the band to Japan for three months.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Two Los Angeles albums while still under contract to Tico
segments.summary: On tour in California a label owner asked them to record, and Morris Levy sent a permission letter for two albums.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Japan tour: factory concerts and gracious audiences
segments.summary: He found Japan receptive; on a twelve-week contract they toured cities and played auditorium concerts for factory shifts as the only American band there.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Latin music in Japan
segments.summary: Japanese radio played Latin music around the clock, loved Los Panchos, Perez Prado and Cugat, and stocked his Tico records.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Pachanga era and records released too late
segments.summary: Back from Japan, work slowed as charanga and pachanga rose; slow record releases made numbers old by the time they came out.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Eight months in Puerto Rico
segments.summary: For sentimental reasons Machito took a ten-man band to a Puerto Rican lounge in 1966 but returned to New York for his family.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Surviving the bugaloo era
segments.summary: Back in New York the band played Casa Blanca and Chez Jose; Machito says a solid professional organization still worked three or four times a week.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: The Cotique bugaloo album
segments.summary: He signed with George Goldner's Cotique, but little came of the album because the label favored young artists.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: "Machito Goes to Memphis" released as Dr. King died
segments.summary: The RCA album's release coincided with Martin Luther King's assassination, so nobody wanted a Memphis theme; it later sold abroad.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Changing personnel and teaching the phrasing
segments.summary: With young jazz sidemen replacing original members, Machito says he teaches them to play tipico with proper attack, dynamics and intonation.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Selecting sidemen: Waymon Reid
segments.summary: He finds sidemen through recommendations; Waymon Reid joined because of the band's top arrangers.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: His partnership with Mario Bauza
segments.summary: They always understood each other, and Machito deferred to Mario's musical decisions.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Gaps between recordings in the 1970s
segments.summary: Between "Solo Machito" in 1969 and later albums, the band kept working; Machito says he lost exposure to the new generation and never counted his albums.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Disc jockeys and playing his records
segments.summary: Machito says he prefers DJs who play his records because they like them, not because they are forced to.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Live bootleg recordings keep the band alive
segments.summary: He agrees recordings made at La Conga and elsewhere educate the public, like showing a diamond rather than keeping it in a vault.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Glad that unauthorized recordings exist
segments.summary: Machito says recordings with Parker, McGhee and Belafonte show people liked the music and preserved great moments.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Royalties, bootlegs and record-company publicity
segments.summary: Chasing royalties is foolish; the Finland trip resulted from Salazar's broadcasts, and company publicity is worth more than small royalties.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Regrets: he would get a conservatory education
segments.summary: He would retire only when God says so but would have gone to a conservatory since education is the simplification of life.

segments.chapter: Later career, tours and reflections
segments.title: Closing: happiness, grandchildren, and no retirement
segments.summary: At seventy, Machito is happy, hopes his grandchildren do well in music, and has no plans to retire; interview ends.
